The claim states that the method 'May miss tiny objects' and is 'sensitive to noisy NeRF inputs (mitigated by anchor-free heads)'. The evidence supports the claim that anchor-free heads mitigate issues with noisy NeRF inputs (Section 5.2 mentions centerness prediction helps when NeRF input is noisy). However, the evidence explicitly states that anchor-free models achieve *higher* AP and recall than anchor-based models, and attributes the success of anchor-free models to handling misalignment and noise. While Figure 7(d) shows 'no proposal for tiny/second-level objects' as a failure case, the text does not explicitly state that the *anchor-free* method specifically 'misses tiny objects' as a general limitation compared to the anchor-based method; in fact, it highlights the superiority of anchor-free models. More importantly, the claim implies a general limitation of the proposed approach (likely the anchor-free one being discussed) regarding tiny objects, but the evidence focuses on the *advantages* of anchor-free models over anchor-based ones. The 'sensitive to noisy NeRF inputs' part is actually mitigated by the anchor-free head according to the text, so saying the method is sensitive is contradicted by the mitigation claim, or at least the evidence shows the anchor-free head *handles* noise well. The 'miss tiny objects' part is supported by Figure 7, but the context of the claim suggests these are limitations of the *overall* method described. Since the evidence strongly supports the mitigation of noise by anchor-free heads and shows high performance, but also shows failure cases for tiny objects, the verdict is partial because not all aspects of the claim are uniformly supported as limitations of the primary method (anchor-free) in the same way.
